newsitem.title: UK: Commodity men go colour-coded as LIFFE gets physical.
newsitem.headline: Commodity men go colour-coded as LIFFE gets physical.

text.p: On a day of culture shock in London markets, a merger with financial futures on Monday paved the way to a glitzy U.S.-style futures trading pit for the staid dealing ring of Europe's oldest tropical products exchange.

The merger deal clinched earlier this year rescued the small 40-year-old London Commodity Exchange (LCE) from likely U.S. takeover, by absorbing it in the vibrant and booming London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE). Participants hope that the merger, which took formal effect on Monday, will take advantage of the dismantling of fram price controls across Europe which may stimulate grains trading.

Meanwhile it struck at tradition. Commodity men found that they had to put on lurid jackets, colour-coded to identify the firm they work for. These are standard issue for the frantic open outcry pits run on the American model and at the bigger, newer LIFFE.
In the old coffee ring, sighed an LCE veteran, business could have been done blindfold. "Everyone knows everyone else's grandparents".

"There was a little resistance to the change in dress code but I think we all accept it as the march of progress," was the nostalgic comment of the head of one commodity brokerage, adding that the merger was the right and best move for the LCE.

"LIFFE gets physical," said the slogan on the red, yellow and blue badges handed out as LIFFE's new commodity division started trading acknowledging that in commodities futures you can actually end up owning sacks of cocoa or coffee. Commercial realities had compelled the $16 million dollar LIFFE offer for the older mainly physical-delivery commodity mart. LIFFE's flagship Euromark futures contract trades 30 times more volume on a good day than, for example, LCE cocoa.

Fifteen years ago leaders of the London money and commodity markets got together to work out how they could combine their skills to set up an exchange mimicking the success Chicago commodity markets had in trading financial futures. From that idea and Chicago's coloured jackets, LIFFE was born.

Freer international grain trade and the dismantling of burdensome and inefficient burocracy in farm policies and prices across Europe will make farm prices less stable, said LIFFE chairman Jack Wigglesworth.

But this volatility is what markets need and will open the way for new contracts to take the price risk away from farmers. LIFFE is now looking at how it can best meet this need and may again turn for advice to Chicago -- the acknowledged leader in grain trade.
